source.title: Resource-constrained Amazons chess decision framework integrating large language models and graph attention
source.authors: Tian-Hao Qian; Zhuo-Xuan Li; Jin-De Cao; Xinli Shi; Hanjie Liu; Leszek Rutkowski

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether a task-specific student trained from a weak model's synthetic supervision can outperform that supervisor, but uses a different training framework and head-to-head win rate rather than the original PGR method.
record.gate_note: The GPT-4o-mini comparisons directly bear on teacher-beating. The ablation comparisons test components of the proposed framework, not whether weak supervision itself beats the supervisor; loss curves likewise do not measure that claim.
record.test_reason: The study trains a small task-specific MCTS/graph-attention agent on GPT-4o-mini's move scores for Amazons. It then reports head-to-head win rates of that student against GPT-4o-mini. This bears on V1's core question, whether a student beats its weak supervisor, in a new setting. The student is not a strong pretrained model fine-tuned on weak labels, no PGR or true-label ceiling is computed, and no unsupervised-search control is run. So this is a new-setting test (T3) rather than a same-question method variant (T2).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors claim the hybrid learns a competitive Amazons policy from noisy GPT-4o-mini scores and beats the teacher at N = 50 (66.5%). They call this 'preliminary empirical evidence' of weak-to-strong generalization and attribute it to graph-based implicit denoising. They concede that handcrafted engines like Invader remain stronger. The conclusion overstates slightly in saying the framework 'consistently outperformed' GPT-4o-mini, given the 45.0% result at N = 30.
record.recipe_differences: The student is a custom MCTS, autoencoder, SGGA, and GAT-AE framework trained using LLM-generated synthetic scores; the evaluation is head-to-head win rate. The study does not use the original PGR calculation or a strong-model true-label ceiling.
record.method_sensitivity: The result changes with search budget: the reported win rate is 45.0% at N = 30 and 66.5% at N = 50.
record.problems: The teacher comparison is reported for one task and one supervisor, over 200 games per reported win rate. Confidence intervals are mentioned but their numerical values are not stated in the text. The study does not measure PGR or compare against a strong model trained on true labels, and its composite framework makes the contribution of weak supervision difficult to isolate.
record.rows_left_out: Ablation comparisons among the hybrid framework, UCTS-AE, SGGA, and GAT-AE are not rows because they compare framework components rather than the weak supervisor or the weak-to-strong effect.

untested.parts: No PGR, no strong ceiling trained on true labels, and no strong pretrained student. Only one supervisor and one task. No control isolating the contribution of weak supervision from the search procedure.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling, or loss-variant comparison against naive training. The ablations compare framework components only.
No variation in supervisor or student size, and no task comparison. Search budget (N = 30 vs 50) is the only varied factor.
No tests of exploitation, distribution shift, or correlated errors.

record.verdict_notes: Main caveat: the student is an MCTS agent playing against an LLM that, per the authors, struggles to track pieces and avoid illegal moves. Search alone may account for the wins. No baseline MCTS without LLM-derived training was played against GPT-4o-mini. How GPT-4o-mini was prompted to play, as distinct from scoring moves, is not described. The ablation win rates (57.5–79.5%) correctly stay out of the rows. The 15–56% 'decision accuracy' improvement in the abstract is not reported in the body.

versions.untested_parts: Tests teacher-beating on Amazons using head-to-head win rate at two search budgets. Does not calculate PGR or compare with a strong model trained on true labels.
No comparison of auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, or loss variants against naive fine-tuning using PGR.
Does not vary supervisor or student model size, compare tasks, or test predictors of PGR. It reports teacher-comparison results at two search budgets only.
Does not test supervisor-checking failures, distribution shift, or correlated errors.
No theoretical conditions for beating a supervisor are tested.

rows.subject: proposed hybrid model
rows.operation_detail: Trained the task-specific framework using synthetic supervision generated by GPT-4o-mini, then evaluated it head-to-head against GPT-4o-mini.
rows.measure: Hybrid model head-to-head win rate against GPT-4o-mini
rows.uncertainty: Confidence intervals are stated to be computed from empirical binomial proportions; numerical interval not stated.
rows.note: The reported win rate is below 50%; the paper describes the result as competitive but does not state a game-level breakdown.
rows.check: Coded reversed. 45.0% over 200 games is within about ±7 points binomial error of 50%, and the authors call it 'competitive'. No interval is given, so this reads as no clear win or loss rather than a demonstrated reversal. The student is a search-based agent, not a fine-tuned strong model.

rows.subject: proposed hybrid model
rows.operation_detail: Trained the task-specific framework using synthetic supervision generated by GPT-4o-mini, then evaluated it head-to-head against GPT-4o-mini.
rows.measure: Hybrid model head-to-head win rate against GPT-4o-mini
rows.uncertainty: Confidence intervals are stated to be computed from empirical binomial proportions; numerical interval not stated.
rows.note: The paper reports this as a win rate for the proposed model against its teacher.
rows.check: Value correct (66.5%, 200 games, N = 50). It cannot be attributed to learning from weak labels alone: no control tests whether the same MCTS with handcrafted features and no GPT-4o-mini supervision also beats GPT-4o-mini.

relationships.condition: Amazons 10×10, hybrid student vs GPT-4o-mini teacher, search budget N = 50
relationships.reason: The student wins 66.5% of 200 games against its supervisor (r2). This holds only without a no-supervision control.
relationships.display_finding: The student won 66.5% of 200 games against its supervisor, although the experiment lacked a no-supervision control.

source_check.reason: r2 reports a 66.5% student win rate over 200 games, supporting the student-over-supervisor comparison in this specialized setting. Stronger pretrained capability recovery and PGR are untested.

relationships.reason: At the smaller budget the student wins only 45.0% (r1), so surpassing the teacher depends on search budget (r1 vs r2).

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r1 shows no demonstrated superiority at the smaller budget: 45.0%, versus 66.5% for r2 at N = 50. The mixed results qualify the comparison by search budget without establishing a reliable reversed effect.

relation.reason: Its own head-to-head experiments directly examine whether the trained framework surpasses its supervisory model.

tranche.reason: The study reports a student-versus-supervisor result in a new setting: a specialized Amazons search-and-graph framework trained using GPT-4o-mini supervision.

source_check.notes: This is an analogue using a custom framework with handcrafted features and search; stronger pretrained student capability and a strong ceiling are not established. No control isolates the contribution of LLM supervision or implicit denoising; the conclusion's claim of consistent superiority over GPT-4o-mini overstates the N = 30 result.

statements.correction: Hybrid versus GPT-4o-mini: 45.0% at N = 30; 66.5% at N = 50; 200 games per result. Section 5.5 states that confidence intervals were computed from empirical binomial proportions; numerical bounds and confidence level are not stated in the text.
statements.problem: The win rates, budgets, and game count are correct. The approximately ±7 percentage-point uncertainty is a checker estimate, not a numerical interval stated in the study; the confidence level is unspecified.
